solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Monitor who comes in to seek coolness?

definitions.text: Monitor who comes in to seek coolness?

blocks.clueFragment: Monitor who comes in to seek coolness?
blocks.note: surface reading: a monitor, the big reptile, slipping indoors out of the heat
setter's reading: the reptile is a decoy, the real subject is a man who idles in bars and clubs hoping to look suave

explanation.surface: A monitor reptile wanders indoors to escape the heat.
explanation.walkthrough: The monitor is a large lizard, and a reptile seeking shade fits the picture; the answer is the idler who haunts fashionable bars posing as cool.
explanation.definitionFit: A lounge lizard is an idle man who frequents bars and parties, aiming for a smooth, fashionable image.

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means turned upside down, so the letters run from bottom to top

blocks.note: to put something down is to set it
as in a right mess, a real mess

explanation.surface: An order to set things straight concerning a Greek monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: SET plus REAL, read upwards, gives LAERTES.
explanation.definitionFit: In Homer, Laertes is king of Ithaca and the father of Odysseus.

clue.text: Sound of rake in large pot

indicators.note: sound of asks for a word that is said the same as the phrase that follows

blocks.note: to rake in money is to earn it

explanation.surface: The noise of a garden rake inside a big pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rake in' reads as a gardening tool inside the pot, but it is one phrase meaning to make money.
explanation.definitionFit: An urn is a large vase or vessel, such as a tea urn.

clue.text: What some doctors do in a convention

blocks.note: first meaning: the work of a family doctor, a GP
second meaning: the usual way things are done, common custom

explanation.surface: Describing what doctors get up to at a conference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convention' suggests a medical conference, but here it means a custom. In Britain a GP (general practitioner) is the local family doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a family doctor's line of work, and also the normal custom or usual procedure in some field.

indicators.note: something shot is ruined or wrecked, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: the letters as written, including the S

explanation.surface: A strange airman's plane has been brought down by gunfire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot down' looks like one phrase about a plane; 'shot' is the anagram signal and 'down' alone is the definition, meaning sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling down means being depressed or dejected, the same mood as being gloomy and dispirited.

blocks.note: surface reading: the closing lines of Lincoln's famous speech
setter's reading: a postal address in the town, whose last item is the American postal number

explanation.surface: Asks about the closing words of Lincoln's Gettysburg Address.
explanation.walkthrough: The speech is a decoy: read 'address' as where letters are sent, and the last line of a US postal address is the five-digit postal number.
explanation.definitionFit: A US mailing address ends with the postal number that Americans call this; Gettysburg is a town in Pennsylvania.

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: rep is short for repertory theatre
ca, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: A critic's review of a play is about to be interrupted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to interrupt' reads as a single phrase meaning soon to interrupt; split it, since about is a piece and 'to interrupt' the signal. Rep is a repertory theatre, staging a rotating season of plays.
explanation.definitionFit: A recap is a brief summary going back over the main points, a short review.

clue.text: A figure of speech matched a figure of speech

indicators.note: of speech means as it is spoken, so the word is wanted for its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: two things that met each other matched up
taken as written
a number, spelt here like the end of a Greek-derived word

explanation.surface: A repeated phrase seems to say one figure of speech matches another.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue looks like a circular definition; the second 'figure of speech' is a spoken number, FOUR, spelt PHOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A metaphor is a figure of speech describing one thing as another, as in 'a heart of stone'.

blocks.note: surface reading: definitions of the word present looked up in a dictionary
setter's reading: present can mean in this place and at this moment, the two senses joined together

explanation.surface: Someone listing what the word present used to mean.
explanation.walkthrough: Present can mean being in this place or at this time; join those two senses and you have a phrase for the present moment. 'Yesterday's' teases that the present is always passing.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the current time and place, which are the two senses of present: in attendance and at this moment.

clue.text: Best shot last one of break

indicators.note: last one of keeps only the final letter of the following word

blocks.note: a pic is a photo, a shot
its final letter

explanation.surface: A sports commentator naming the finest shot at the end of a snooker break.
explanation.walkthrough: Snooker words, shot and break, lead the solver astray; the shot is a photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: The pick of the bunch is the best one, the choicest item in a group.

clue.text: Revolting man, inventor, bank has to back

indicators.note: going back means the following letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: James Watt, Scottish engineer of steam-engine fame
to bank on someone is to rely on them

explanation.surface: A list describing a disgusting man, an inventor and a bank in retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' suggests disgusting, but means rebelling: Wat Tyler led the Peasants' Revolt in England in 1381.
explanation.definitionFit: Wat Tyler was leader of the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381, so literally a man in revolt.

clue.text: Hanger-on goes for wee, initially confused

indicators.note: the opening sounds of two words get mixed up, swapping places as in Dr Spooner's slips

blocks.note: goes for means picks or chooses, and wee means little; swap their opening sounds

explanation.surface: A clingy companion heads for the toilet, muddled from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes for wee' suggests a toilet trip, but it is two separate words, picks and little, whose first letters swap.
explanation.definitionFit: A lickspittle is a fawning toady, the sort of servile follower who hangs around someone powerful.

blocks.note: first meaning: what a theatre helper does for an actor who forgets their words
second meaning: quick, acting with speed and without delay

explanation.surface: Organising supply routes efficiently on an exploring journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply lines' and 'expedition' suggest a military or exploring trip; expedition here means speed, and supply lines means feeding actors their words.
explanation.definitionFit: To prompt is to remind an actor of forgotten lines; prompt also describes acting with speed and readiness.

blocks.note: surface reading: no longer bothered about anything
setter's reading: medical care in former times, an archaic word for medicine

explanation.surface: Someone shrugging that they no longer care.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means indifference, but read literally it is healing of the past; the answer is an old word for medicine or the art of healing.
explanation.definitionFit: Physic is an archaic term for medicine and the medical profession, the caring of earlier times.

clue.text: Unopened beer and glass smashed for charity

indicators.note: unopened means the opening letter of the word is taken away
smashed things are broken into pieces, so the letters are reassembled in a new order

blocks.note: beer without its first letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pub fundraiser where beer goes unopened and glasses get broken.
explanation.walkthrough: The beer loses its first letter before being mixed with the glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Largesse is generous giving to others, the open-handed spirit of charity.

indicators.note: a word crossing another stretches across it, so it surrounds the other piece

blocks.note: to stew is to fret
as means while
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Officials fret as they cross the street.
explanation.walkthrough: The road sits inside the word for while, after the word for worry.
explanation.definitionFit: Stewards are officials who manage events such as race meetings or concerts.

clue.text: Undertaker is featured in advert, right?

indicators.note: featured in means appearing inside, so the short word goes in the middle

blocks.note: a promo is a promotional advertisement
taken as written
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A funeral director appears in a commercial, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undertaker' suggests funerals, but means one who undertakes to do something, a person making a promise.
explanation.definitionFit: A promisor, in legal language, is the party who undertakes an obligation, giving a binding promise.

clue.text: Words repeated on top of Petri dish?

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a mantra is a phrase chanted over and over
its first letter

explanation.surface: Words written over a Petri dish in a laboratory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Petri dish' looks like a lab item; dish is the definition, slang for an attractive person, and the question mark flags the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A mantrap is slang for a seductive woman, and a dish is slang for someone very attractive.

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so these letters are read backwards

blocks.note: a pot is a prize fund, a purse
per means for each, as in one per person

explanation.surface: A handbag is handed back in exchange for a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purse' suggests a handbag, but here it means prize money, the pot in a game or contest.
explanation.definitionFit: A topper is a top hat, the tall silk hat of formal dress.

indicators.note: synthetic means artificially made, so the letters are manufactured into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A river sustains industry that uses a man-made chemical.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, a piece that supports another sits beneath it, so R comes after the rearranged word. 'Synthetic compound' looks like the definition, but synthetic is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A polymer is a chemical compound built from many repeated units, like nylon or plastic.

clue.text: Old magical character I found east of Black Country

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
a rune is a letter of an ancient alphabet credited with magic power
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rune found east of the Black Country, an industrial area of the English Midlands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black Country' reads as the Midlands region; split it, and black gives B while country is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Brunei is a small, oil-rich sultanate on the island of Borneo in South-East Asia.

blocks.note: standard cricket abbreviation
to go over a road is to go across it

explanation.surface: Bumping into a pirate while running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run across' reads as meet by chance, but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Rover is an old word for a sea robber, a buccaneer roving the seas.

clue.text: Car maker designing software I call revolutionary

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns right around, so the word is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: CAD is computer-aided design
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An automotive engineer hails a radical piece of design software.
explanation.walkthrough: CAD, I, then CALL backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadillac is the American luxury car brand owned by General Motors.

indicators.note: concealed means kept within, so the letters lie inside the neighbouring words

blocks.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A body-snatcher's hidden secret condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a noun, a condition; it is the verb to assert.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to state firmly or declare something to be true.

indicators.note: weaving interlaces threads into a new pattern, so the letters are reworked into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to weave fabric into a flawless cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: The textile picture suits the answer, but the material and do are just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tailor-made is ideally suited, as if cut by a tailor to fit exactly.

indicators.note: cutting into a word means slicing into its middle, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: OK means allowed
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Clearing part of a woodland with permission.
explanation.walkthrough: A goes inside OK.
explanation.definitionFit: Oak is a hardwood timber prized for furniture and building.

clue.text: For kind of club outing, look over ground

indicators.note: to look over something is to cast an eye around it, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: a trip is an outing
to leer is to look slyly
deck means the ground, as in hit the deck

explanation.surface: A golf club outing to inspect the course.
explanation.walkthrough: Club here is a club sandwich, not a golf or social club; 'For' simply links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A club sandwich built in three layers is called a triple-decker, so it is one kind of club.
